name: Jade Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, 43, and I lead our awkward home and shop repair calls with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence. I'm among the strongest fault finders here, and I keep a little box of failed fittings because showing the damage can teach more than telling somebody to be quicker. My partner Ellis delivers furniture, our children are eight and eleven, and we've a mortgage and fourteen months of expenses saved; my pay is high for the trade and plenty of electrical firms work nearby. I use AI occasionally for a checked draft note after somebody has shown me the method works, and I like teaching a sound diagnosis, but dislike seeing an apprentice apologise for time the job genuinely needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small useful tool can earn its place without changing our whole story. I'd keep the checked note draft when it helps. The apprentice still needs someone to explain the damaged fitting, not another announcement about the office becoming clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the mortgage and ordinary family costs, and fourteen months saved gives us a substantial margin. I feel secure about my work and money in this picture. There are plenty of local firms I could approach, but I don't need to chase them to get next month's bills paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the repair calls and checking completed crew work now and through the next year. I'd keep my occasional note drafts checked against the readings and use the failed fittings during explanations inside ordinary paid work. I wouldn't turn the fourteen-month reserve into a new saving claim or buy another tool to make the quiet story more exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased I can enjoy a job finished properly. I can spend an evening with Ellis and the children without adding a course because the news said I ought to be preparing. There's room in our budget for an ordinary surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use a failed fitting when teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the apprentice what failed and ask what evidence changed the first diagnosis. Then I'd explain which part of the check mattered, rather than just tell a story about my own experience. Being good at finding faults doesn't automatically make me good at explaining them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend more of the reserve because this picture felt secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep the existing reserve and ordinary budget. A quiet technology story isn't a reason to make a new commitment every week. Keeping money already saved is our present position, not extra saving from a change.

say: I'd keep **small useful tools** without asking the crew to adopt a new story about the whole trade.
I'd value **proper explanations** for apprentices more than another announcement about clever office software.
think: Our wages and **fourteen-month reserve** make the mortgage and ordinary family costs feel secure.
Plentiful **local employers** offer options without requiring a search to pay next month's bills.
do: Keep **repair leadership** and completed-work checks through the next year.
Continue checked note drafts and practical explanations inside **ordinary paid work**, retaining the existing household budget.
feel: **Calm and settled**, with financial room for ordinary surprises and evenings that don't become compulsory preparation.
S0.quote: Being good at finding faults doesn't automatically make me good at explaining them.
fieldNote: Her **security** rests on high pay, covered costs, substantial savings and plentiful employers, without making expertise protection against all change.
Existing **cash and routine tools** remain ordinary continuity, not new saving or a new AI-learning action.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs, checking completed work and using familiar checked note drafts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union branch the saved minutes ought to help people learn, not just squeeze another visit into the van. I'd ask for paid monthly fault clinics, meetings to discuss real repair faults, for office and site staff, so the booking team could see what a real awkward job involved too. I'd test the search tool after someone showed me it worked, not because a sales sheet said it understood our trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair wage and Ellis's physical work look secure over the next few years. I'm uneasy about faster office targets reaching people who haven't had time to learn a new routine. I can afford to ask a question at the meeting, and I don't want that confidence restricted to people with a reserve like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd learn the approved AI job-history search only free during paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours maintained, after a colleague demonstrated eight completed jobs. During the first year I'd take a proposal for two paid clinic hours monthly to the union branch, without reducing anyone's normal weekly wages or hours. I'd keep leading repairs and treat both the clinic proposal and the tool trial as requests until the employer actually agreed the terms in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the way the gain is shared, but secure about my own living. I'd be interested to see whether finding an old job faster helped us explain the next one. I don't need a software demonstration to become a loyalty test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a result from the search tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the returned record with our original readings and the actual repair before using it. A similar-looking board doesn't mean the fault was the same. If the search kept returning misleading examples, I'd stop the trial and show the errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would different staff actually do at a fault clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentices could ask why the diagnosis changed, and office staff could ask what travel and access the estimate missed. Nobody would get permission to do electrical work from attending a meeting. The point is understanding the paid day, with qualified checks still where they belong.

say: I'd seek **shared learning time** from office savings rather than simply another visit squeezed into the rota.
I'd include **office and site staff** in paid fault clinics about the real working day.
think: Our **near-term physical wages** look secure, so this isn't a plan to replace an immediately missing income.
I'm uneasy about **faster targets** and want learning confidence to depend on agreed terms rather than personal savings.
do: Learn **AI job-history search** after eight demos only with written approval, free access, paid practice and normal weekly wages and hours maintained.
Seek **two paid clinic hours** monthly for all staff, preserving normal weekly wages and hours.
Keep **repair leadership**, treating both proposals as unagreed until written terms are actually accepted.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, interested in tested improvements without making enthusiasm a loyalty test.
S1.quote: A similar-looking board doesn't mean the fault was the same.
fieldNote: The **new search tool** is distinct from her occasional existing note drafts, and its trial preserves fees, paid time, wages and hours.
The **collective clinic proposal** is an actual shared request, not individual teaching relabelled organising or a new electrical qualification.

steps.text: Inspect eight completed-job demonstrations before learning the AI job-history search
Learn job-history search only with written approval, free access, paid time and normal weekly pay/hours maintained
Seek two paid clinic hours monthly for all staff with normal weekly wages and hours maintained
Keep paid repair leadership while proposed terms remain unagreed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch thinking AGI arrives in 2028 and capable robots follow around 2031 for physical work. We should negotiate while people still have hours, including the office staff facing the earlier change. My master electrician's licence doesn't make the rest of the crew invisible or my own work permanently safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid repair hours could shrink when robots handle the physical tasks, and Ellis's delivery wage could change too. Fourteen months saved gives us room to respond, not guaranteed income for the rest of our working lives. I'd be anxious about losing two useful wages close together, even though we have choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd replace our planned hotel holiday with local day trips, using the lower spending to keep room in the ordinary budget rather than call it a new deposit. In 2029 I'd help the branch seek the two monthly paid clinic hours with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged, adding a request for staffing notice before cuts. I'd keep actual paid repairs while talks continued and review both household wages quarterly, without assuming any proposal was agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to refuse a rushed expensive answer. I can try a smaller holiday without telling the children the house is in danger today. I want the reserve to give us choice, not give me a reason to stop checking the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refused the clinic proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current paid arrangement and ask the branch to show members the actual answer. I'd still explain faults within ordinary crew work, but I wouldn't announce that everyone had won two new paid hours. A meeting cannot pay a wage the employer hasn't agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the smaller holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd chosen day trips to leave room for decisions if work changed. I'd ask what the children wanted to do locally rather than make the holiday a punishment for a forecast. A smaller holiday isn't a lesson in blaming somebody else's job.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from capable physical robots around 2031.
I'd negotiate before cuts, including **office staff** rather than use the site team's later date for everyone.
think: Both household wages could lose **physical paid hours later**, including my own repairs.
The **fourteen-month reserve** gives choices without guaranteeing income throughout the rest of our working lives.
do: Replace the **hotel holiday** with local day trips now, using the lower cost for budget room rather than assumed new saving.
Seek **paid clinic hours** and staffing notice in 2029, preserving normal weekly wages and hours.
Keep **actual paid repairs** and review both wages quarterly, counting no unagreed proposal as protection.
feel: **Anxious with choices**, able to cut a discretionary cost without treating today's home as already at risk.
S2.quote: A meeting cannot pay a wage the employer hasn't agreed.
fieldNote: Her **personal income risk** is explicit despite strong finances; the reserve creates time to respond rather than assumed permanent immunity.
The **holiday change** reduces spending without inventing a deposit, and requested clinic hours preserve wages and hours while remaining unagreed.

steps.text: Replace the planned hotel holiday with local day trips
Seek two paid clinic hours monthly in 2029 with normal weekly wages/hours unchanged; request staffing notice
Keep actual paid repairs and review both household wages quarterly after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us find out whether a paid clinic changes the actual day rather than just collect good intentions. Thinking work changes in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. We'd still need office staff in the discussion from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages and household costs look secure over the next few years, with time to test an arrangement while I keep earning. I'm uneasy about later physical work, not expecting an immediate collapse of our money in this picture. More warning gives me time to notice an unhelpful proposal before defending it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the same local day-trip holiday plan now and help the branch seek two paid clinic hours monthly without reducing normal weekly wages or hours. If agreed, we'd compare corrected handovers and repeat faults before and after each clinic, sharing the actual results with staff. In 2032 I'd keep paid repairs and review both wages quarterly, revising the proposal rather than assume a clinic protected jobs from capable robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, with room to test and change my mind. I'd like staff to say when the clinic wasn't helping. Being fair to people doesn't require pretending my first proposal was perfect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the clinic added work but did not improve the handovers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the branch and employer to revise or stop it under the written agreement, without anyone donating unpaid hours or losing normal weekly pay. I'd want that safeguard written before it started. The failed fitting should teach us something, including when our teaching plan wasn't useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you review household needs in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032 our children would be fourteen and seventeen, so Ellis and I would check their real school and family arrangements rather than copy today's diary. I wouldn't put their possible future wages into our budget. I'd still take responsibility for the household plan with my partner.

say: I'd use **five years** to test whether paid learning improves the actual working day.
I'd include **office staff early**, keeping their thinking-work date distinct from later physical robots.
think: Our **near-term wages** and costs look secure while I continue earning and test a proposed arrangement.
I'm uneasy about **later physical work**, with time to reject an unhelpful proposal rather than defend it automatically.
do: Choose **local day trips** now and seek two paid clinic hours monthly with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged.
Require **written trial safeguards** before starting, allowing revision or stopping without unpaid hours or lost normal weekly pay.
Keep **2032 paid repairs**, checking clinic results and both household wages quarterly without assuming future job protection.
feel: **Uneasy** and willing to revise, while financially secure enough now to test an imperfect idea honestly.
S3.quote: Being fair to people doesn't require pretending my first proposal was perfect.
fieldNote: She measures **actual handovers** and repeat faults, treating her preferred shared-learning proposal as an experiment rather than a moral certainty.
The **pre-start safeguard** protects paid time and normal wages, while the household review correctly ages the children to fourteen and seventeen.

steps.text: Replace the hotel holiday with local day trips
Seek two paid clinic hours monthly with normal weekly wages and hours maintained
Require written clinic revision and stopping terms beforehand, preserving paid time and normal weekly wages
Keep paid repairs and review both household wages quarterly after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years gives us time to make paid learning ordinary instead of a personal emergency. I'd still ask who can afford to practise in the current arrangement. I don't want the longest warning to mean the longest unpaid homework for people already stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when capable robots follow around 2039. Our own wages and fourteen-month reserve make the next few years secure, but I can't claim the same jobs last forever. I'm uneasy about that later question without living as if the next mortgage payment has already failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the day-trip holiday plan and seek the same paid clinic, with normal weekly wages and hours maintained and written protection against unpaid extra work or lost wages if it changed or stopped. We'd review household wages and actual costs quarterly, checking real commitments as the children became adults. In 2037 I'd keep paid repairs and help revise the clinic from actual results, counting no employer agreement or future child's income before it existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later work, but with room for a normal Saturday with the family. I can ask for change without turning every quiet afternoon into evidence that I should be doing more. I'd like the children to see learning as part of life rather than a permanent alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What commitments would you check when the children were adults?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be nineteen and twenty-two in 2037, so we'd check where they actually lived and what help had been agreed. I wouldn't keep a school-pickup duty in a plan for adults, or assume they no longer needed anything. Their possible wages aren't ours to use before a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer never agreed the clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present paid job and ask the branch to show staff the actual written answer. I'd continue ordinary explanations within paid crew work, not donate the rejected clinic in my evenings. More time doesn't turn a refusal into an agreement.

say: I'd make **paid learning** an ordinary shared work issue instead of a permanent individual emergency.
I'd ask who can afford **practice time**, without using a long warning to justify unpaid homework.
think: Our **near-term wages** and reserve feel secure, while the same jobs are not guaranteed for life.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings beyond later robots without claiming today's mortgage or future children solve that need.
do: Keep **local day trips** and seek the paid clinic with normal weekly wages and hours maintained.
Require **written stop safeguards** against unpaid extra work or lost normal wages before any agreed clinic begins.
Keep **2037 paid repairs**, reviewing actual costs, wages and adult household commitments quarterly rather than assume agreement or children's income.
feel: **Uneasy but secure now**, leaving space for family life while seeking a practical shared change.
S4.quote: More time doesn't turn a refusal into an agreement.
fieldNote: She **ages the children** into adulthood before discussing 2037 commitments, with neither frozen school duties nor assumed child income.
The **paid clinic conditions** remain explicit across time, including written revision or stopping protection and no unilateral unpaid substitute after refusal.

steps.text: Replace the hotel holiday with local day trips
Seek two paid clinic hours monthly with normal weekly wages and hours maintained
Require written clinic revision and stopping terms beforehand, preserving paid time and normal weekly wages
Keep paid repairs and review actual adult household commitments and wages quarterly after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both our physical wages could be squeezed around 2031 before we've checked many alternatives. Agreed paid learning, unchanged weekly wages during any trial and staff seeing the actual evidence would help. I want the apprentice to get a paid explanation, not inherit my confidence as another unpaid task.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether somebody with savings still has a reason to want shared protection. I do, because a person's chance to learn shouldn't depend on whether their partner can cover a missed wage. My own margin gives me room to speak; it doesn't make everybody else's margin imaginary.

headlineQuote: I want the apprentice to get a paid explanation, not inherit my confidence as another unpaid task.
portrait: Jade, **43**, leads difficult repairs with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, and is among the firm's strongest fault finders.
She has **higher pay**, fourteen months saved, plentiful local employers, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with furniture-delivery partner Ellis.
She uses **AI occasionally** after proof, checking records against real readings and testing a distinct search tool only within protected paid work.
Her **paid clinic proposal** includes office and site staff, preserved wages and hours, and written safeguards rather than assuming an employer agreement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before capable robots could squeeze both physical household wages around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Agreed paid learning**, unchanged trial wages and staff access to actual results would help without assuming a proposal already protects jobs.
